guidance.heading: Choose on working load limit, not on size
guidance.body: Every part here is rated by its working load limit: the heaviest load it may carry in service. Start from the load and how it is rigged — the number of legs, the sling angle, how the weight is shared — and choose the component whose WLL covers the worst-loaded leg. Two parts of the same nominal size can carry very different loads: a Grade 80 hook and a carbon hook of the same frame, or a shackle loaded straight and one side-loaded. Proof and breaking loads are test figures; never select on them.

standards.heading: Design factors and patterns
standards.body: A lifting component is rated with a design factor between its WLL and its minimum breaking load. Alloy chain and its fittings are typically rated at 4:1, wire rope slings at 5:1, and forged shackles at 5:1 or 6:1 depending on the standard they are made to. Each size table shows the ratings the manufacturer publishes, in the unit they are rated in, and each product page names the pattern or standard its range follows — DIN 580, EN 13411-3 or the US G-209 and G-2130 patterns, for example.

service.heading: What ships with it
service.body: Every consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — put it on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange before we quote.

items.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
items.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

items.q: Can Grade 30, 43 or 70 chain be used for lifting?
items.a: No. Proof coil (Grade 30), high test (Grade 43) and transport (Grade 70) chain are made for tie-down, towing and general duty. Overhead lifting with chain calls for alloy chain — Grade 80 or Grade 100 — with fittings of the same grade.

items.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
items.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

items.q: How do I read an Indus lifting part number?
items.a: IH-LR, then the family code, then the size. Inch sizes are written in hundredths of an inch (075 is 3/4″, 025X200 is 1/4″ × 2″), metric sizes in millimetres (10MM, M16), and capacities in tonnes (0T5 is 0.5 t). A trailing -C or -A marks the carbon-steel and alloy-steel versions of the same hook or link.

guidance.heading: Match the hardware to the load path
guidance.body: Rate every piece in the load path for the load it actually sees. A shackle or eye bolt pulled off its axis carries less than its vertical rating; a hook must seat the sling in its bowl, not on its tip; and a master link has to take every leg of the sling at once. Where a range comes in carbon and alloy steel of the same frame, the alloy version carries more — the size table lists the two as separate rows with their own ratings.

items.q: Which shackle do I need — anchor (bow) or chain (dee)?
items.a: A chain (dee) shackle is for a straight, in-line pull. An anchor (bow) shackle has a rounder body that accepts more than one sling or a pull at an angle to the pin. For a permanent or long-term installation choose a bolt-type shackle, whose nut and cotter pin cannot unscrew in service; a screw-pin shackle suits rigging that is made and broken often.

The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

guidance.heading: A rope is only as strong as its termination
guidance.body: Wire rope is chosen on construction, core and tensile grade: more wires per strand bend more easily over a sheave, a steel core (IWRC) resists crushing and adds strength, and a higher grade carries more for the same diameter. Then the termination decides what the assembly can carry — a thimble protects the eye from kinking, clips must be the right number, the right way round and torqued, and a ferrule has to be pressed with the die made for it.

standards.heading: Standards for terminations
standards.body: Ferrule-secured eyes are covered by EN 13411-3 (the successor to DIN 3093) and lifting-grade wire rope clips by EN 13411-5 (which replaced DIN 1142). DIN 741 malleable clips are not intended for lifting terminations. Thimbles follow DIN 6899 and BS 464, or the US standard and extra-heavy patterns.

items.q: How many wire rope clips does an eye need?
items.a: It depends on the rope diameter and the clip type, and the clip maker's table is the authority. The U-bolt goes on the dead (short) end and the saddle on the live end — "never saddle a dead horse" — and the nuts are re-torqued after the first load.

items.q: What is the difference between a fibre core and a steel core?
items.a: A fibre core (FC) makes the rope more flexible; an independent wire rope core (IWRC) resists crushing on a drum and carries a higher breaking load for the same diameter. The size tables give both where the manufacturer publishes them.

guidance.heading: Lifting chain and everything else
guidance.body: Only alloy chain — Grade 80 or Grade 100 — is for overhead lifting, and it must be used with fittings of the same grade and size. Grade 30 proof coil, Grade 43 high test and Grade 70 transport chain are for tie-down, towing and general duty; DIN 763, 764 and 766 link chain is for fencing, guarding and light mechanical duty. items.q: Can I mix Grade 80 chain with Grade 100 fittings?

guidance.heading: Angle changes everything
guidance.body: A sling's rating is for a straight vertical pull. As the angle between two legs opens, each leg carries more of the load, so a two-leg sling at 90° between its legs is rated well below twice a single leg — the endless-sling table shows the drop directly. Choose the sling on its rated load for the angle you will actually use.

standards.heading: Wire rope slings
standards.body: Wire rope slings are commonly made to EN 13414-1, which rates them at a 5:1 design factor. The soft-eye sling tables give the WLL at both 5:1 and 6:1 so you can work to the factor your site specifies.

items.q: Are cable socks for lifting?
items.a: No. A cable sock is a pulling grip — it draws cable or hose through a duct or over rollers. Its breaking load is a pulling figure, and it is not rated for suspending a load.

guidance.heading: Capacity, lift and headroom
guidance.body: Choose a hoist on its rated capacity, the lift you need and the headroom you have: the hook-to-hook distance on the table is the height the hoist itself takes up. A trolley must match both the hoist's capacity and the flange width of your beam, and a plate clamp must match the plate thickness it grips — both ranges are in the size tables.

items.q: What is the difference between a push trolley and a geared trolley?
items.a: A push trolley is moved by pushing on the load; a geared trolley is driven by a hand chain, which gives finer positioning and is easier with heavier loads.

items.q: Can a snatch block be used for lifting?
items.a: Yes, within its rated load — but the load on the block is not the load on the rope. With the rope turned through 180° the block carries about twice the line pull, so rate the block, its hook or shackle and its anchor point for that.

guidance.heading: Bow or dee, screw pin or bolt
guidance.body: A chain (dee) shackle takes an in-line pull; an anchor (bow) shackle accepts several slings or a pull at an angle. Screw-pin shackles are for rigging made and broken often; bolt-type shackles, with a nut and cotter pin, are for long-term or permanent installations where a pin could otherwise work loose. Side-loading a shackle reduces what it may carry, so allow for it when the pull is not in line with the body.

items.q: What do G-209, G-2130 and G-213 mean?
items.a: They are widely used US pattern numbers: G-209 is a screw-pin anchor shackle, G-2130 a bolt-type anchor shackle, and G-213 a round-pin anchor shackle. Shackles sold to a pattern share its dimensions, so they interchange in an existing rigging plan.

items.a: A ratchet binder tensions gradually and releases under control, so it suits operators who tension and release often. A lever binder is quicker but stores energy in the handle and must be released with care.

items.q: Which fibre should I choose?
items.a: Polypropylene floats and is economical; polyethylene is similar and resists abrasion; nylon stretches and absorbs shock, which suits mooring; polyester stretches least and holds up best in sunlight. State the diameter, construction and length on the RFQ.

guidance.heading: Bolted, welded or swivelling
guidance.body: A swivel lifting point turns and pivots to line up with the sling, so it keeps its rating at an angle where a fixed eye bolt would not. Bolt-on points need the thread engagement and tightening torque the maker states; weld-on points need a qualified welder, a base material that suits the weld and inspection before first use. Pad eyes and deck eye plates are fixing points: check whether a size is rated for lifting or only for lashing before you rig from it.

items.q: Can I lift at an angle from an eye bolt?
items.a: A plain eye bolt is rated for a straight pull along the thread axis; at an angle its capacity falls sharply. A shoulder eye bolt seated fully takes an angled pull at a reduced rating. Where the pull will be angled or will change direction, use a swivel lifting point, which turns to follow the sling.

items.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
items.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

guidance.heading: A retainer, not a load pin
guidance.body: These pins keep a clevis pin, bolt or hitch pin in place; they do not carry the load. Size them to the hole they pass through and the pin they retain, and choose stainless steel where they will see weather or washdown. A retaining pin that is bent or has lost its spring should be replaced, not refitted.

items.q: What is the difference between a lynch pin and an R-clip?
items.a: A lynch pin has a spring ring that snaps over the end of the pin it retains; an R-clip is a single piece of spring wire that clips through a cross-hole and over the pin. Both are quick to fit and remove. A wire lock pin adds a locking wire that swings over the end so it cannot shake out.

guidance.heading: Use Grade 100 fittings with Grade 100 chain
guidance.body: Grade 100 fittings carry about a quarter more than Grade 80 fittings for the same chain size, so a Grade 100 sling must be built from Grade 100 chain and fittings throughout — a single Grade 80 part sets the rating of the whole sling. Match each fitting to the chain size it is made for, and select on the WLL for the sling configuration.

standards.heading: Rated at 4:1
standards.body: Grade 100 chain and its fittings are rated with a 4:1 design factor between working load limit and minimum breaking force. Each size table shows the WLL and breaking load the manufacturer publishes for the fitting.

items.q: Can I mix Grade 80 and Grade 100 components?
items.a: You can, but the sling is then rated as Grade 80: the weakest component sets the working load limit of the whole assembly. To use the Grade 100 rating, every component in the load path must be Grade 100.

guidance.body: Stainless link chain resists corrosion in marine, food and architectural use, but most of it is not lifting chain: a DIN link chain is published with a breaking load for general duty. For overhead lifting, use chain and fittings that carry a working load limit for lifting, and treat a breaking-load-only rating as not rated for lifting.

items.q: Is stainless steel chain as strong as alloy lifting chain?
items.a: No. Stainless steel chain of the same size is considerably weaker than Grade 80 or Grade 100 alloy chain, and most stainless link chain is published with a breaking load rather than a lifting rating. Choose it for corrosion resistance, and use rated alloy chain where the job is lifting.

guidance.heading: Protect the sling, rate it for the hitch
guidance.body: Synthetic slings are light and grip a load without marking it, but they cut on sharp edges — use edge protection wherever the sling bends over a corner. The WLL marked on the sling is for a straight vertical lift; a choker hitch reduces it and a basket hitch increases it, depending on the angle. Inspect the label and the cover before every use and retire a sling with cuts, burns or a missing label.

standards.heading: Colour code and design factor
standards.body: Under EN 1492 the colour of a polyester sling marks its rated capacity: violet 1 t, green 2 t, yellow 3 t, grey 4 t, red 5 t, brown 6 t, blue 8 t and orange 10 t and above. Textile slings are rated with a 7:1 design factor.

items.q: Round sling or webbing sling?
items.a: A round sling has a continuous core of load-bearing yarn inside a protective cover, so it is flexible and moulds to the load. A flat webbing sling spreads the load over a wider bearing surface and sits flat under the load. Both are rated the same way; choose on how the load is shaped and handled.

guidance.heading: Pick the termination for the rope and the duty
guidance.body: A spelter socket, poured correctly, develops the full breaking strength of the rope and is the termination for heavy lifting and structural rope. Swage terminals are pressed onto the rope with the right die; swageless terminals are assembled by hand and suit cable railing and rigging where a press is not available. Match every terminal to the rope diameter and construction it is made for.

items.q: What is the difference between an open and a closed spelter socket?
items.a: An open socket ends in a jaw with a pin, so it connects straight to a lug or plate; a closed socket ends in an eye that takes a shackle or pin. Both are filled with resin or zinc to bond the broomed rope end.

guidance.body: A ratchet strap tensions a load down to the vehicle; it is not a sling. standards.heading: Ratings on a tie-down
standards.body: Load-securing equipment is labelled with its lashing capacity (LC) under EN 12195-2, or in US practice with a working load limit of one third of its breaking strength. items.q: How many ratchet straps do I need?
items.a: Enough that their combined rating covers the load and how it can move under braking, cornering and acceleration — it depends on the load, the vehicle and the lashing method. Use at least two for any load, and follow the load-securing rules that apply where you operate.

guidance.heading: Rate the bollard for the line, and the deck for the bollard
guidance.body: A bollard is chosen on the safe working load of the lines it will take and the standard the vessel or berth is built to. Its rating assumes it is welded or bolted to structure that can carry the load, so the deck or quay reinforcement matters as much as the casting. The tables give each size with its published load and principal dimensions against the drawing.

items.q: What does the nominal size of a marine bollard mean?
items.a: For a double bollard to GB/T 554, ISO 13795 or JIS F 2001, the nominal size is the diameter of the pillar in millimetres; the standard sets the safe working load and dimensions that go with it. Quote the standard, the type and the nominal size on the RFQ.

guidance.heading: Size a fender on energy, not on size
guidance.body: A fender is selected on the berthing energy it must absorb and the reaction force the hull and the structure can take. The tables list published energy absorption and reaction at rated deflection where the maker gives them, with the principal dimensions against the drawing. For a berth design, send the vessel sizes, berthing speed and structure details and we will confirm a fender and its fixings.

items.q: What is the difference between energy absorption and reaction force?
items.a: Energy absorption is how much of the vessel's berthing energy the fender takes up as it compresses; reaction force is the load it passes back into the hull and the quay. A good selection absorbs the energy required while keeping the reaction within what the hull and structure can carry.

faqs.question: Round sling or webbing sling?
faqs.answer: A round sling has a continuous core of load-bearing yarn inside a protective cover, so it is flexible and moulds to the load. A flat webbing sling spreads the load over a wider bearing surface and sits flat under the load. Both are rated the same way; choose on how the load is shaped and handled.

faqs.question: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faqs.answer: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a lynch pin and an R-clip?
faqs.answer: A lynch pin has a spring ring that snaps over the end of the pin it retains; an R-clip is a single piece of spring wire that clips through a cross-hole and over the pin. faqs.question: What do G-209, G-2130 and G-213 mean?
faqs.answer: They are widely used US pattern numbers: G-209 is a screw-pin anchor shackle, G-2130 a bolt-type anchor shackle, and G-213 a round-pin anchor shackle. Shackles sold to a pattern share its dimensions, so they interchange in an existing rigging plan.

faqs.question: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faqs.answer: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

A shackle joins a sling, hook or chain to a lifting point and opens with a removable pin. Built to the European pattern. Stainless steel 304 or 316 bow shackle, polished / electrophoretic coating.

Sizes and ratings

12 sizes, 5 mm to 14 mm. Minimum breaking load 91 to 748 kN. Available as: bow, dee. Every size has its own Indus part number in the table below, with the loads in the unit the manufacturer rates them in.

Ordering

faqs.question: What is the working load limit?
faqs.answer: 1 to 6 t, depending on size, as the manufacturer rates it. The WLL is the most the part may carry in service; proof and breaking loads are test figures and never working limits.

faqs.question: Round sling or webbing sling?
faqs.answer: A round sling has a continuous core of load-bearing yarn inside a protective cover, so it is flexible and moulds to the load. A flat webbing sling spreads the load over a wider bearing surface and sits flat under the load. Both are rated the same way; choose on how the load is shaped and handled.

faqs.question: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faqs.answer: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faqs.question: Do the parts come with a test certificate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. For third-party certification or witnessed proof testing, say so on the RFQ.

faqs.question: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faqs.answer: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faqs.question: Can I lift at an angle from an eye bolt?
faqs.answer: A plain eye bolt is rated for a straight pull along the thread axis; at an angle its capacity falls sharply. A shoulder eye bolt seated fully takes an angled pull at a reduced rating. Where the pull will be angled or will change direction, use a swivel lifting point, which turns to follow the sling.

faqs.question: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faqs.answer: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.
